title: Looking back: the stories
hook: the palace, the tree, the Deer Park, the sal trees

segments.voice: Yesterday: ehipassiko, and your line, come and see. Did you practice one thing without calling it anything, and watch what it did? Day three hundred twenty-six, and the big lookout begins.

At the end of a year, lots of people scroll back through their phone's photos. A birthday. A beach. A hospital waiting room. A dog. Things you'd forgotten, and things you never will. You're near the top of the first mountain now. For six days, we're going to turn around and look at the path behind you, one piece at a time. First, the stories: a whole life, from a palace to a grove of trees, that you've walked with since the start of the second camp. Today: looking back.
screen: `SCROLLING BACK THROUGH THE YEAR.` → `NEAR THE TOP OF THE FIRST MOUNTAIN.` → `FIRST, THE STORIES.`

segments.voice: The palace. A prince named Siddhattha, the one whose aim succeeds, raised in three palaces, one for each season, with every comfort. Then four sights on the road with Channa: an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and a wanderer with a calm face. One night he looks in once at his sleeping wife Yasodhara and their newborn son, rides out on Kanthaka, and cuts off his hair by a river. The tree. Six years of starving himself, down to a handful of beans a day, until he remembers a quiet afternoon under a rose-apple tree as a boy. Sujata's bowl of rice. Eight handfuls of grass for a seat. I will not rise. Mara's army, and his hand reaching down to touch the earth. At dawn, awake. The Deer Park. Five old companions agree to ignore him, and then, as he comes near, they stand up. He teaches the middle way and the four truths, and Kondañña sees. The sal trees. Eighty years old, walking still, he eats his last meal from Cunda the smith, and lies down between two sal trees that bloom out of season. His last words are about change and care; the last day of this year hears them in full. And all around the four scenes, the people: Kisa Gotami and the mustard seed, the man with the finger garland who was told, I have stopped, you stop, and the Jataka animals, the hare in the moon and the golden goose. You don't need to remember every detail. What stays is the shape: comfort, a question, a long search, a seat under a tree, a teaching given away, a good death. The stories stay.
screen: `THE PALACE — FOUR SIGHTS.` · `THE TREE — I WILL NOT RISE.` · `THE DEER PARK — THEY STOOD UP.` · `THE SAL TREES — THE LAST WORDS.` · then, large: `THE STORIES STAY.`

segments.voice: Before the sit, choose one story from the year, whichever comes to mind first. Retell it to yourself from memory, silently, in a few sentences, as if to a child at bedtime. Don't check anything. Whatever you remember is what stayed. Then let the story settle, and sit with the breath, the way he sat under the tree. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. The palace, the tree, the Deer Park and the sal trees: the whole life, from comfort to a good death, as it stays with you.
Your line: the stories stay. Today, tell one of this year's stories to someone else, a friend, a child, a partner, in your own words. Day three hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Buddhists retell the Buddha's life at festivals such as Vesak, in temple murals and in children's classes, and many keep images of the four great scenes: the birth, the awakening, the first teaching and the passing away.

match.prompt: match each scene of the life.

myth: the five companions at the Deer Park refused to listen to him
they agreed to ignore him, then stood up to greet him as he came near.
the Buddha's last words urged diligence
a call to keep going with care; the full line closes the year on day 331.
the sal trees bloomed out of season at his passing
the story says they flowered as he lay between them.

fork.setup: you're the prince, starving yourself in the forest after six years. a memory comes back: a quiet afternoon under a rose-apple tree. what do you do?
options: push the memory away and fast harder.
accept a bowl of rice and try the quiet way.
fork.reveal: he took Sujata's rice, found a seat under the tree, and awoke by dawn: the middle way between comfort and starving.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit bodhi: awakening, the heart of the life story, and the name of the tree he sat under.

trapdoor: what you thought: a legend about a prince.
what it means: a life with a shape: comfort, a question, a search, awakening, teaching, a good death.
what a scholar hears: the full life appears only in later works such as the Nidanakatha and Buddhacarita; the early discourses tell it in scattered pieces (e.g. MN 26, MN 36, DN 16).
